The overnight story is energy: Brent is at 102.56 (-2.58%) and WTI at 89.38 (-3.48% as reported) because Iran says it has received a US response to its seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Qatar-mediated proposals are under review (Al Jazeera, CBS). The Revolutionary Guard, though, says fighting continues daily in Hormuz, and at least three commercial vessels have been hit, so the de-escalation trade is fragile. Tuesday's cash session was a soft grind lower: SPX -0.17% to 7670.84, Nasdaq -0.09%, Dow -0.26% and Russell 2000 -0.35%, with VIX steady at 16.04. Rates bull-steepened. The US 2Y fell 5.4bp to 4.8765%, the 10Y was flat at 5.2362%, and the 30Y rose 1.9bp to 5.5658%. That is consistent with a market that has priced a hawkish Warsh Fed in the front end and keeps adding term premium at the long end against a -5.441% of GDP budget deficit. Futures quotes are not in today's feed (n/a), so this AM read uses prior closes and live FX/commodities. Sentiment is complacent but not euphoric. Credit spreads are tight (IG 0.82, HY 3.03), and the event risk is concentrated in tonight's Micron print and the path to the late-October FOMC.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Growth is beating value and defensives are not providing shelter. In the US, over one month, Info Tech (+4.1%) and Comm Services (+2.61%) are the only clear gainers. Materials (-6.95%), Financials (-6.83%), Cons Discretionary (-6.71%), Utilities (-6.57%) and Real Estate (-6.23%) are all down more than 6%. Industrials fell 4.37% and Cons Staples 2.2%. The bond-proxy sectors (Utilities, Real Estate, Staples) are suffering with a 5.24% 10Y, which marks this as a rates-driven de-rating rather than a classic risk-off rotation. Yesterday's +1.14% bounce in Utilities on the 2Y rally is a one-day relief move within a -8.06% YTD trend. Energy, still the YTD leader (+34.64% US, +30.7% global), fell 0.89% on the day and 0.73% over the month as crude eases on Hormuz talk. Globally the pattern matches: Info Tech +3.68% 1m and +34.13% YTD, while Materials (-7.78% 1m), Cons Discretionary (-6.68%) and Real Estate (-6.07%) lead the declines. Global Cons Discretionary is -9.45% YTD, signalling consumer strain beyond the US.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.88 vol points (58th percentile of the 31 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 106.6 (77th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 107bp (steeper by 36bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.24 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 64/100 — Sticky, with broad breadth. Core PCE at 3.34% sits well above core CPI at 2.4%, and the underlying measures (median CPI 2.58%, sticky CPI 2.74%, median PCE 2.72%) are clustered at 2.5-2.75%. That is not re-accelerating, but not converging to 2% either. The Dallas Fed distribution shows 52.2% of the PCE basket rising above 3% (computed from 29.9 + 13.0 + 9.3) and only 25.8% falling, so price pressure is widespread rather than concentrated. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score is not in today's feed (n/a) and is rendered separately. On balance this supports Warsh's hawkish lean.

⚔️Iran War

Diplomacy is moving, but the war is not over. Iran says it has received a US response to its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and its senior leaders are reviewing Washington's counter-proposal after Qatari mediation. Tehran's seven-day plan for a ceasefire and a phased Hormuz reopening depends on the US meeting conditions from the mid-June memorandum of understanding, which collapsed after several weeks. President Trump has publicly rejected the proposal and has said the war will end 'very soon' without giving details. On the ground, the IRGC says 'military conflict' continues daily in Hormuz, and a maritime agency reports at least three commercial vessels hit by projectiles. Treasury Secretary Bessent says Iran may deliver its last ~15 million barrels of loaded oil to China within two weeks, leaving Tehran little to trade. Inside Iran, food and beverage inflation has reached 127.5%. The IRGC is also appealing to US voters ahead of the Nov 3 midterms. Market read: this morning's oil decline prices the talks, but continued ship strikes make the move reversible.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Lean toward a 25bp hike at the October FOMC (inference). Warsh held rates at his first meeting on Sep 16, but more officials signalled a hike ahead. Markets price better-than-even odds of an October hike and most traders see one by December. In his Jackson Hole speech and at his press conference, he repeatedly called financial conditions 'not restrictive'. Our read is that tight credit spreads (IG 82bp) and a record-high equity backdrop give him cover to act.

~1 YEAR

Expect one to two further hikes plus a continued push to shrink the balance sheet over ~12 months (inference). This is based on Warsh's long-standing criticism of QE and his 'regime change' agenda, which includes five new policy-review task forces and a balance-sheet overhaul that is meeting internal resistance. Forbes reports markets bracing for two more hikes in 2026. Cuts are unlikely unless financial conditions tighten sharply or the labour market breaks (4.1% unemployment, 197k claims).

Warsh's on-record framework puts financial conditions at the centre: he stressed them three times at Jackson Hole and three more times at his first press conference. He attributes higher 10Y yields to economic strength, competition for capital and geopolitics rather than to Fed credibility problems, which means he is unlikely to lean against 5%+ long yields. CNBC notes this could put the Fed 'at odds' with the Treasury. That tension matters for the long end given the -5.441% deficit. The near-term and one-year paths above are inferences from his statements and market pricing, not his stated plans.
